agent.definition.text: A system in which the model decides the next action, a program runs the tools and returns the results to the model, and the loop continues until the task is done or a stop condition triggers.

harness.definition.text: The program wrapped around the model: it builds requests, runs tools, manages context, budgets, and stop conditions, and records the evidence of each run. The runner in each lesson is a minimal implementation of it.

tool-calling.definition.text: The idea that the model does not perform actions itself: it names a tool and its arguments, the program actually runs the tool, and the result goes back to the model.

json-schema.definition.text: A specification for describing the structure of JSON data. A tool definition uses it to state each parameter's fields, types, and required items, so the model can generate arguments and the program can validate them.

tool-result.definition.text: The real return value after the program runs a tool, sent back as a tool message and linked by tool_call_id to the call that triggered it.

message-history.definition.text: The sequence of system, user, assistant, and tool messages sent with every request. The model has no hidden memory; it sees only what is carried here.

agent-loop.definition.text: The repeating cycle "request the model → run tools → append results → request again", guaranteed to end by stop conditions such as a round limit.

trace.definition.text: The events recorded in order during one run: requests, responses, tool calls, results, and so on. It is used for checking and replay; replay does not run anything again.

allowlist.definition.text: Only tools or operations registered in advance may run. When the model asks for a name that is not on the list, the program refuses to run it and returns an error.

stop-condition.definition.text: A rule that decides when a run ends, such as getting a final answer, reaching a round or budget limit, or hitting an unrecoverable error.

acceptance-criteria.definition.text: Completion conditions written in advance that can be checked against actual results. They decide whether the task is really done, instead of relying on the agent's claim that it is.

structured-output.definition.text: Requiring the model to output an agreed JSON structure, then having the program check the format and business rules. A valid structure does not mean the content is correct.

tool-description.definition.text: The text in a tool definition that is written for the model to read: the tool's description and each parameter's description. The model uses it to decide whether to call the tool and how to fill in the arguments. It is only an explanation and grants no permission to run.

validator.definition.text: A program, independent of the model, that checks output or run evidence against rules written in advance. When it judges whether a task is done, it is also called the acceptance checker. The model's self-assessment cannot replace it.

application-state.definition.text: Structured data kept by the program, such as the task goal, completed steps, evidence, and terminal state. It is managed separately from the message history sent to the model.

context-window.definition.text: The maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one request. Input and output share this limit.

context-budget.definition.text: The capacity limit allocated to each part of one request (instructions, history, tool results, output). When it is exceeded, something has to be cut or compressed.

context-compression.definition.text: Rewriting old context shorter before continuing to use it: assembling a record by rules, clearing old tool results, or having the model write a summary. The result must still follow the message protocol, and whether the key information survived has to be checked separately.

token.definition.text: The basic unit into which the model splits text. Context limits and billing are counted in tokens; character counts are only a rough estimate.

usage.definition.text: Data such as token consumption that the provider reports in its response. When it is not returned, write "not reported"; do not pass off a local estimate as usage.

prompt-tokens.definition.text: The prompt_tokens field in usage: the token count of everything sent to the model in this request, including the system prompt, message history, tool definitions, and the markers added by the chat template. It is usually larger than the text you can see.

completion-tokens.definition.text: The completion_tokens field in usage: the number of tokens the model wrote this time. A reasoning model's reasoning content is usually counted here too, so it can be large even when the answer is short; check the provider's documentation.

memory.definition.text: Information the program stores for the model and supplies again later. A conversation does not make the model itself remember anything.

persistent-memory.definition.text: Memory kept in external storage across runs and sessions. Its source, retrieval, updates, expiry, and deletion all need to be managed.

chunking.definition.text: Cutting a long document into pieces that carry source information, so they can be retrieved and fit into limited context.

vector-retrieval.definition.text: A retrieval method that turns text into vectors and finds relevant pieces by semantic similarity.

hybrid-retrieval.definition.text: Combining keyword and vector retrieval results and re-ranking them, to get both exact matches and semantic closeness.

rag.definition.text: First retrieve relevant pieces from source material, then give the pieces to the model as evidence for generating the answer.

citation.definition.text: A source note in the answer that points to the retrieved piece actually used. The citation must really exist and support the claim it is attached to.

agentic-rag.definition.text: RAG in which the agent decides, from the evidence so far, whether to rewrite the query, keep retrieving, or stop and answer. It needs call and time budgets.

human-in-the-loop.definition.text: Pausing the run at a key step so a person can approve, edit, or reject before it continues. Often used together with checkpoints.

checkpoint.definition.text: A saved state of a run at a given step, so the task can resume from it after a pause, failure, or restart.

idempotency.definition.text: The property that running the same operation once or many times has the same effect. It is needed when retrying or resuming tools that write.

transient-failure.definition.text: A failure whose cause goes away by itself, such as a lock wait that timed out or a service that is briefly overloaded; trying again a little later may succeed. Invalid arguments and business-rule refusals are not transient.

backoff.definition.text: Waiting for a while after a failure before retrying. Exponential backoff grows the wait 1x, 2x, 4x up to a cap, usually scaled by a random factor so that many callers spread out.

idempotency-key.definition.text: A unique name the caller gives one write operation before its first attempt and sends unchanged with every retry; a store that has seen it returns the first result instead of running again.

compensation.definition.text: When a multi-step write fails halfway, a reverse write that undoes a step that already took effect, such as refunding a credit already taken. It keeps the history and must itself be safe to repeat.

evaluation.definition.text: Measuring an agent's performance with a fixed question set, criteria defined in advance, and an independent validator, and keeping failure records to compare versions.

dev-set.definition.text: The fixed case set you run again and again while improving an agent, to find problems and compare changes. Scores tuned against it run optimistic, so a holdout set has to confirm them.

holdout-set.definition.text: Cases set aside in advance, never looked at or tuned against while improving. They run once a version is chosen, to check whether the gains on the development set hold.

paired-analysis.definition.text: Two versions run the same cases and are compared case by case, looking only at the cases whose verdicts differ and which way they moved, instead of subtracting two pass rates.

regression.definition.text: After a change, a case that used to pass no longer does. A regression check reruns old cases on the new version, especially failures that were fixed before.

observability.definition.text: The ability to locate problems and compare costs afterward, by recording run data such as requests, tools, state, latency, and usage.

span.definition.text: A single timed step in a trace, such as one model request or one tool execution. Several spans make up one trace.

correlation-id.definition.text: An identifier that ties a summary record to its raw events, such as a run id, a round or a call id; with it, one row of a report leads back to its request or tool call.

end-to-end-latency.definition.text: The total time of a run from start to finish, including the program overhead between spans; the time of a single span is its step latency.

prompt-injection.definition.text: Instructions hidden in source material, web pages, or tool results that try to change the agent's behavior. External text must be treated as data only; permissions are controlled by the program.

function-calling.definition.text: The mechanism by which a provider API implements tool calling: the request declares functions and their parameter schemas, and the response returns structured tool call proposals.

mcp.definition.text: An open protocol that lets an agent discover and call the tools and resources offered by external services through one common protocol.

multi-agent.definition.text: A structure in which several agents with different roles work together on a task. It is worth adopting only when a controlled experiment shows a gain.

sub-agent.definition.text: An agent that a main agent delegates to: it does a subtask in its own context and returns the result.

role-switching.definition.text: One agent puts on a different system prompt at each stage while the message history stays shared; the role changes, but the run identity and the context are not separated.

context-isolation.definition.text: Each agent works only in its own context and sees only what is handed to it; this cuts out unrelated information and also loses whatever was not handed over.

handoff-package.definition.text: Everything handed to another agent: the task, the confirmed facts and constraints, and the material to work on; whatever is left out, the receiver does not know.

coding-agent.definition.text: An agent that reads and writes files, runs commands and tests in a code repository, and decides its next step from the results, such as the agent modes of Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot. Each product's capabilities and permission settings follow its own documentation.

prompt-caching.definition.text: The provider reuses already-processed results for the beginning of a request that matches an earlier request word for word, which lowers latency and cost. What the model sees does not change; how much was hit is whatever the response reports.

progressive-disclosure.definition.text: Providing only a directory or summary first and loading the details when needed, to save context.

context-rot.definition.text: The longer the context, the weaker the model's ability to retrieve an earlier piece of information accurately. Information still being in the window does not mean it will be used.

attention-budget.definition.text: Treating the amount of information a model can attend to effectively as a limited resource, and deciding from that which content goes into the context.

plan-and-execute.definition.text: A control pattern that first generates a complete plan, then executes it step by step, replanning from the results when needed.

reflection.definition.text: Having the model check its own output against review comments or validation results, find problems, and then revise.

orchestrator-workers.definition.text: A workflow pattern in which an orchestrator splits a task, assigns the parts to several workers to run, and then combines their results.

evaluator-optimizer.definition.text: A workflow pattern in which one role generates a result and another evaluates it and gives feedback, looping to improve until it passes or reaches the iteration limit.

sandbox.definition.text: An isolated execution environment that limits the files, network, and resources that code or commands can access. An ordinary local process is not a sandbox.

artifact.definition.text: In the A2A protocol, the structured result returned when a task finishes, such as a file or data.

stop-sequence.definition.text: A string specified in the request; when the model's output reaches it, the provider cuts the output off. Often used to make a text-protocol model stop after it writes an action.

observation.definition.text: The result returned to the model after a tool has really run. Only the program can supply it; an Observation written by the model itself is made up.

prompt-chaining.definition.text: Splitting a task into several model calls in a fixed order, where each step's output is the next step's input and the program can check between steps.

routing.definition.text: Having the model classify the input first, then the program hands it to a different processing path by category. A category that cannot be recognized goes to a fallback path.

offline-test-mode.definition.text: A mode that does not connect to a model provider: the lesson's fixtures.py generates deterministic model responses for each request, and tools still really run. It is only for automated tests, and its results do not represent a real model.

replay.definition.text: Stepping through a recorded run event by event. It only moves a cursor; it does not request the model again or run tools again.

context.definition.text: Everything the model can see in one request: the system rules, message history, tool definitions, and tool results. The model cannot see information outside the request.

structured-error.definition.text: Returning data such as ok=false, error_type, and error when a tool fails, instead of raising an exception or giving a default value, so the model can read why it failed.

terminal-state.definition.text: The last state of a run or task, such as completed, error, or cancelled. Once reached it cannot be left, and the reason must be written down. A terminal state of completed does not mean the task was done correctly.

task-card.definition.text: A task contract written before execution: goal, input scope, outputs, evidence, failure handling, and stop conditions. Acceptance looks only at this card and the actual evidence.

completion-claim.definition.text: The "done" statement an executor hands in at the end, with an answer and evidence references. It is only a claim to be checked and is not evidence itself.

call-budget.definition.text: The upper limit on model calls allowed in one run, taken from max_rounds in the lesson manifest. When it is used up the platform stops, and parallel branches share the same allowance.

controlled-experiment.definition.text: A comparison that changes one condition and keeps everything else fixed, so the difference can be attributed to that condition. A single result is only one observation.

message-protocol.definition.text: The rules multi-turn messages must follow, for example each tool call must be followed by a tool message with the same tool_call_id. When the rules are broken, the provider may reject the request or may answer anyway.

react.definition.text: Reasoning + Acting: the model alternates between writing reasoning and an action, the program runs the action and returns an observation, and the model then decides the next step. It can be implemented with a text format or with native tool calling.

text-action-protocol.definition.text: The model writes its thought, tool name, and arguments in an agreed format inside ordinary text; the program parses out the action, runs it, and pastes the result back.

todo-list.definition.text: A list of steps and their statuses that the model maintains itself with a dedicated tool, to track progress. It is the model's own statement and cannot replace acceptance.

memory-recall.definition.text: Taking records out of the memory store by rules such as scope and putting them into this request. Being saved in the store does not mean being recalled.

workflow.definition.text: A structure in which the program fixes the steps and branches in advance and the model only fills in the content of each step. It contrasts with an agent loop, where the model decides the next step.

parallelization.definition.text: Sending independent subtasks to the model at the same time and combining the results in the program. It saves waiting time but does not reduce model calls or usage.

gate.definition.text: A check the program runs between two adjacent steps. If it fails, the run stops at that step and does not pass the failing result on.

tokenizer.definition.text: The component that splits text into tokens. Each model has its own tokenizer, so the same text can come out as different token counts.

fault-injection.definition.text: Deliberately constructing wrong inputs or abnormal responses to check whether a program's error-handling paths work as expected.

baseline.definition.text: The original or simplest approach used as the reference in a controlled experiment; a new approach's gain only holds when compared against it.

ablation.definition.text: Removing just one part of an experiment while keeping the rest unchanged, then comparing results, to confirm what that part does.

keyword-screening.definition.text: A rough check that looks only at whether the output contains specified words or numbers. A hit does not mean it is semantically correct; the conclusion must be checked against the original text.

temperature.definition.text: A sampling parameter: lower values lean toward the highest-probability token and make answers steadier; higher values spread out more. It does not change the information in the request, and setting it to 0 does not guarantee identical output every time.

fixture.definition.text: Data or a simulated component fixed in advance for tests. Each lesson's fixtures.py generates deterministic model responses per request; it is used only for offline tests and is not a run record.

confusion-matrix.definition.text: A table that counts samples by "human annotation category × predicted category": the diagonal holds the correct ones and the other cells show which two categories get confused.

wall-clock-time.definition.text: The actual time elapsed from start to finish. With parallel execution it can be shorter than the sum of the individual task times.

openai-compatible.definition.text: An interface that follows the OpenAI Chat Completions request and response format, offered by most providers. This platform builds its messages in that format.

annotation.definition.text: The correct answer or category that a person writes for a sample in advance, used to measure model output. Annotations themselves can also be wrong.

stable-prefix.definition.text: The part at the start of every request that stays word-for-word the same, such as rules, tool definitions, and fixed material. Dynamic content goes after it so that prompt caching can reuse it.

cached-tokens.definition.text: The number of input tokens, reported by the provider in usage, that reused the cache in this request. Field names differ between providers; when the response does not report it, record it as not reported, not as 0.

skill.definition.text: A set of instructions written for the model, with a name and a description. The model uses the description to decide when to use it and reads the full text only when needed.

optimistic-concurrency.definition.text: Writing without a long-lived lock: the write carries the version number that was read, and if it differs from the store's current version, the write is rejected and the current value stays unchanged.

message-role.definition.text: The role of each message in the message list: system is the rules for the model, user is the user's words, assistant is the model's reply, and tool is a tool result.

system-prompt.definition.text: The system-role message at the start of the message list, giving the model its identity, rules, and output requirements. It is just text the model reads: it can influence how the model answers, but it cannot be enforced the way a permission check in a program can.

finish-reason.definition.text: The finish_reason in a response, saying why the output stopped: stop means the model finished writing or hit a stop sequence in the request; length means the output was cut off at its limit; tool_calls means it proposed tool calls.

sampling.definition.text: For each token it writes, the model draws one from the probability distribution over candidate tokens according to a rule. So sending the same request twice can give different answers.

large-language-model.definition.text: A language model pre-trained on massive text and then trained for dialogue, often shortened to LLM. It reads a sequence of tokens and writes an answer by predicting the next token one at a time; it does not remember conversations or perform actions by itself, and only outputs text. Every "model" in the course means this.

model-parameters.definition.text: The large number of values a model learns in training, which determine the probabilities it gives after reading an input. Requests, conversations, and saved memory never change them; only further training does. They are also not call parameters such as temperature in a request.

pre-training.definition.text: Training a model on massive text to predict the next token. The model learns language patterns and a lot of knowledge from it, but that knowledge stops at the cutoff date of the training data and does not include private material that was never public.

reinforcement-learning.definition.text: A way of learning in which a program tries things repeatedly in an environment and adjusts its behavior by reward: it sees a state, chooses an action, and gets a reward. It is also used to train models to follow instructions and use tools.

autoregressive.definition.text: How a model generates: it predicts only the next token each time, appends it to the end of the text, and predicts the next, until it writes a stop marker or reaches the length limit.

base-model.definition.text: A model that has only been pre-trained and can only continue text. Given a question, it may write more questions instead of answering.

instruct-model.definition.text: A model trained further on dialogue and instruction data on top of a base model, so it answers by message role and follows instructions. Following instructions is a tendency in probability, not a guarantee in a program.

chat-template.definition.text: The formatting rule that assembles a role-tagged message list into one piece of text with special markers, for the model to continue. It differs between models and is usually applied by the provider on the backend.

special-token.definition.text: A token reserved in the tokenizer's vocabulary to mark where a message begins, what role it has, and where it ends. Ordinary text usually cannot produce them; when the model writes the special token that means the end, the provider stops generating.

knowledge-cutoff.definition.text: The last date covered by the data the model was trained on. The model has not seen what happened afterward, so the program must put that material into the context or provide a lookup tool.

web-search.definition.text: A chat-application feature: when needed, the program searches the web and puts what it finds into the context, and the model answers from it. The model cannot go online itself; this is essentially tool calling plus retrieval. Each product's exact approach follows its own documentation.

hallucination.definition.text: Output that is fluent and confident but contradicts the facts or the material given. It comes from continuing text by probability, with no built-in fact check; it can only be reduced, and prompts cannot eliminate it.

rubric.definition.text: A set of criteria written in advance, judged one by one during review. The more specific and checkable each criterion is, the more stable the review result.

reasoning-model.definition.text: A model that generates reasoning content first and then gives the answer. Some providers put the reasoning in a separate field such as reasoning_content, and the tokens it uses count toward completion tokens.

tool-call-proposal.definition.text: The tool name and arguments the model writes in tool_calls in its response. It is only a proposal that has not run; the program decides whether to run it.

llm-judge.definition.text: A model that judges whether another model's output is acceptable against a rubric written in advance. It also fluctuates and has preferences of its own, so its judgments must first be compared with human conclusions.

iteration-limit.definition.text: The maximum number of review rounds in a revision loop. At the limit no more revision is requested and the stop reason is recorded; stopping at the limit does not mean passing.

goal-loop.definition.text: A loop in which an independent validator checks after each execution; if it fails, the run retries with the reason, and stops when it passes or reaches the attempt limit.

namespace.definition.text: A label in the memory store that partitions records and, together with the key, identifies one record. It only decides which partition to look in and does not verify the caller's identity.

state-machine.definition.text: A set of states plus allowed transitions. The program changes state only through the transition table, and any transition not in the table is rejected.
